newsitem.title: UK: UK nationalist parties proclaim socialist values.
newsitem.headline: UK nationalist parties proclaim socialist values.

text.p: Support for higher taxes and closer European integration would be considered electoral suicide by many British politicians standing at national polls on May 1, yet the parties fighting for Scottish and Welsh independence think they are vote-winners.

At a news conference in London on Tuesday, Scottish Nationalist Party (SNP) leader Alex Salmond and Plaid Cymru (Party of Wales) president Dafydd Wigley said they were united not only by their nationalist agenda but also by a committment to socialist values abandoned by most British parties.
"Plaid Cymru and the SNP remain committed to restoring full employment and defending the interests of those in need," Wigley said. "Compassion and concern rest at the heart of our communities."
The SNP and Plaid Cymru hold four seats each in Britain's outgoing parliament and both say they are confident of increasing this tally on May 1.

A poll in the Scotsman newspaper on Tuesday put SNP support in Scotland at 23 percent, second only to Labour who polled 42 percent. Surveys in Scotland and Wales have consistently shown significant support either for more self-government or complete independence.

The growing clamour for self-rule has led the main opposition Labour Party to promise to give Wales and Scotland a referendum on greater autonomy. The ruling Conservatives are firmly against any form of independence.
Labour leader Tony Blair outraged many nationalists by playing down the powers of Scotland's proposed parliament.
Wigley and Salmond said they expected to win votes from Labour as a result and also because Blair's modernised "new Labour" party had ditched much of its socialist dogma.

"New Labour has given up practically every social and economic policy that brought them strong support in Scotland and Wales at successive elections," Salmond said. Both Wigley and Salmond said they were happy to call themselves socialists, a label which Blair has tried to play down.

While the Conservatives and Labour have made a point of pledging not to raise taxes, Plaid Cymru says it would increase income tax by two percent if it governed Wales. The SNP says it would cut taxes for the poorest in Scotland while making high-earners pay more.

The nationalist parties also stand apart from the Conservatives and Labour on Europe. Both of Britain's main parties have declined to commit themselves to a single currency and plan to hold a referendum before joining.
But Salmond said the people of Scotland and Wales were very positive about European integration.
"It would be a tragedy for Wales if the EU went ahead with the single currency and the UK stayed out," Wigley said.
